lesson.title: Guardrails in code
lesson.subtitle: Rules the model can’t talk its way past

video.title: Guardrails in code
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds, one recurring teacher character. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Mr Joseph Mwangi — computer studies teacher, Kenya (main character)
Ms Amina Bello — primary teacher, Nigeria (cameo)
Narrator — the Darsi voice, talking to the student (warm, peer to peer)

chapters.label: A model that learned to ask

scenes.visual: A list: It learned to ask first; “Yes, send it.”, alone; A made-up message.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Darsi Tiny learned to ask before it sends a message. So, job done, the model is safe? Then someone typed: yes, send it, with nothing before it. It made up a message, and tried to send it!

scenes.animation: The Darsi mark pops in; the title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: guardrails, the safety rules you write in code.

scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: A model’s good habits are learned, and learned behaviour can fail. Darsi Tiny refuses the harmful requests it was trained on. But reworded in new ways, twenty-eight percent of the English ones got a tool call instead. So real safety goes in your code.

scenes.visual: A list: The model proposes an action; Run it; Ask a person; Block it.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: A guardrail is a rule in code that checks an action before it runs. It doesn’t guess, and it can’t be talked round. The model proposes; the guardrail decides: run it, ask a person, or block it.

scenes.visual: Code typed out on a card: ALLOWED = ["weather", "route"] …
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.on_screen_text: Rule one: only the tools it needs
scenes.narration: Rule one: an allow-list. A weather helper needs the weather tool, not attendance and not messages. If the model asks for a tool off the list, block it.

scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.on_screen_text: Rule two: yes to this exact message
scenes.narration: Rule two: actions wait for a person. The app shows the exact message and asks: yes or no? It remembers exactly what was approved. A yes to one message is not a yes to another.

scenes.visual: A list: Does the class exist?; 25:00 is not a time; Names from the request; 9Z became 9C.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Rule three: check every detail before a tool runs. Is six B a class that exists? Is twenty-five o’clock a real time? Did every name come from the request or a result? Darsi Tiny once copied nine Z as nine C.

scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Quick check! The person said yes to: the trip is cancelled. Now the model proposes a different message: pay the fees today. What should the guard return?

scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Ask again. The yes was for a different message, so it doesn’t count. Compare the exact details, not just the word yes, and the model can’t send something nobody approved.

scenes.visual: Code typed out on a card: verdict = guard(name, args, ok) …
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Rule four: log everything. Every proposed action, what the guard decided, and who approved it. When something goes wrong, the log shows what happened.

scenes.visual: A list: Choose what it may do; Approve a message to Mrs Mensah; Check off: what gets through?.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: In the lab, choose what Darsi Tiny may do: read only, ask first, or allowed. Send a message to Mrs Mensah, and approve it. Then switch the code check off, send yes, send it, alone, and see what gets through.

scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Your turn. Darsi Tiny learned to ask before sending. So where should the final check live?

scenes.visual: Summary points: Only the tools it needs; A yes to the exact action; Check details, log all.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.on_screen_text: Only the tools it needs · A yes to the exact action · Check details, log all
scenes.narration: In the app’s code, with a person’s yes. Remember: allow only the tools a task needs. Run an action only after a yes to that exact action. Check every detail, and log everything.

scenes.visual: A list: Write the rules on paper; Which tools?; What waits for a yes?; Test with a friend.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Try it yourself: on paper, write the guardrails for a homework-reminder agent. Which tools does it need? Which actions wait for a yes, and which details must you check? Then test them on a friend’s sneakiest requests.

checkpoints.prompt: The person approved “The trip is cancelled.” The model now proposes “Pay the fees today.” What should the guard return?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — the yes was for a different message. Comparing the exact details stops a model from sending something nobody approved.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — a yes counts only for the exact message it was given for. Ask about this one.

checkpoints.prompt: Darsi Tiny learned to ask before sending. Where should the final check live?

options.text: In the app’s code, with a person’s yes

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — learned behaviour can fail, as “yes, send it” on its own showed. A rule in code, with a person’s yes, can’t be talked round.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — training makes asking likely, not certain. The final check belongs in code, with a person’s yes.
